questions.prompt: A computer is an electronic device that:
options: Only sends data to another device or user
questions.explanation: The course defines a computer as "an electronic device that stores and processes data."

questions.prompt: In general, hardware comprises:
options: The invisible instructions that control the computer
Only the programs stored in memory
Only the data processed by the CPU
The visible, physical elements of the computer
questions.explanation: Hardware comprises the visible, physical elements of the computer; software is the invisible instructions.

questions.prompt: Software provides:
options: The invisible instructions that control the hardware and make it perform specific tasks
The visible, physical elements of the computer
The roads that carry data and power between components
The circuit case that connects all parts of the computer
questions.explanation: Software provides the invisible instructions that control the hardware and make it perform specific tasks.

questions.prompt: Network interface cards (NICs) and modems are examples of:
questions.explanation: The course lists communication devices "such as modems and network interface cards."

questions.title: Match each group of computer components with its examples

questions.prompt: A computer's components are interconnected by a subsystem called:
questions.explanation: The course states that a computer's components are interconnected by a subsystem called a bus.

questions.title: Match each term with its description

pairs.right: The brain of the computer; retrieves and executes instructions
Stores data and program instructions for the CPU to execute
Subsystem that interconnects the computer components
Circuit case that connects all parts of the computer together

questions.prompt: The central processing unit (CPU) is described as:
options: The system of roads among the components
The circuit case that connects all the parts
The permanent store of programs and data
questions.explanation: The course calls the CPU "the brain of a computer."

questions.prompt: The CPU retrieves instructions from _____ and executes them.
questions.explanation: The CPU retrieves instructions from memory and executes them.

questions.prompt: The CPU speed is measured in:
questions.explanation: The course states that the CPU speed is measured in megahertz (MHz).

questions.prompt: 1 megahertz equals:
questions.explanation: 1 megahertz equals 1 million pulses per second.

questions.prompt: Memory is used to:
options: Store data and program instructions for the CPU to execute
Store programs and data permanently, even when the power is off
Send data from the computer to another device or user
Connect all of the parts of the computer together
questions.explanation: Memory is to store data and program instructions for the CPU to execute.

questions.prompt: A memory unit is:
options: A set of tracks on a disk
A system of roads among the components
questions.explanation: The course defines a memory unit as an ordered sequence of bytes, each holding eight bits.

questions.prompt: Each byte in memory holds:
questions.explanation: A memory unit is an ordered sequence of bytes, each holding eight bits (a bit = 0 or 1).

questions.prompt: What happens to the current content of a memory byte when new information is placed in it?
options: It is moved to a storage device
It is moved to the next byte
It is kept together with the new information
questions.explanation: The current content of a memory byte is lost whenever new information is placed in it.

questions.prompt: A program and its data must be brought to memory before they can be executed.
questions.explanation: The course says a program and its data must be brought to memory before they can be executed; storage devices only keep them permanently.

questions.prompt: Memory is volatile because:
options: The content of a byte is lost when new information is placed in it
Information is lost when the power is off
It permanently stores programs and data
It sends data from the computer to the user
questions.explanation: The course says memory is volatile because information is lost when the power is off.

questions.prompt: Where are programs and data permanently stored?
questions.explanation: Programs and data are permanently stored on storage devices.

questions.prompt: Programs and data are permanently stored in memory and are moved to storage devices when the computer uses them.
questions.explanation: It is the opposite: they are permanently stored on storage devices and moved to memory when used.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares memory and storage devices?
options: Storage devices are volatile, while memory stores programs and data permanently
Memory is volatile, while storage devices store programs and data permanently
Both memory and storage devices lose information when the power is off
Both memory and storage devices store programs and data permanently
questions.explanation: Memory loses information when the power is off (volatile); storage devices store programs and data permanently.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three main types of storage devices?
questions.explanation: The three main types of storage devices are disk drives, CD drives, and tape drives.

questions.title: Match each type of storage device with its examples

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a storage device?
questions.explanation: Hard disks are disk drives, one of the three main types of storage devices. Memory is separate from storage devices and is volatile.

questions.prompt: An output device is any device used to:
options: Send data from a computer to another device or user
questions.explanation: An output device is any device used to send data from a computer to another device or user.

questions.prompt: An output device is any device used to send data to a computer.
questions.explanation: That describes an input device. An output device sends data from a computer to another device or user.

questions.prompt: Which two factors determine the quality of the display?
options: The dot pitch and bus speed
questions.explanation: The resolution and dot pitch determine the quality of the display.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an output device?
questions.explanation: Output devices send data from a computer to another device or user, such as monitors and printers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an output device?
questions.explanation: An output device sends data from a computer to another device or user (monitors, printers, speakers). A keyboard is an input device.

questions.prompt: An input device is any hardware device that:
options: Sends data from a computer to another device or user
questions.explanation: An input device is any hardware device that sends data to a computer.

questions.prompt: Input and output devices let the user:
questions.explanation: The course states that input and output devices let the user communicate with the computer.

questions.prompt: The most common input devices are:
questions.explanation: The most common input devices are keyboards and mice.

questions.prompt: A printer is an input device because it sends data to a computer.
questions.explanation: A printer is an output device; input devices such as keyboards and mice send data to a computer.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an input device?
questions.explanation: An input device sends data to a computer (keyboards, mice, scanners). A monitor is an output device: it displays information.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an input device?
questions.explanation: An input device sends data to a computer; the scanner is shown among the input devices. Projectors, speakers, and printers are output devices.

questions.prompt: A microphone is classified as:
questions.explanation: The microphone appears among the input devices because it sends data to the computer.

questions.title: Match each device with its group

questions.prompt: The Von Neumann architecture is the foundation for:
options: Only computers that use parallel processing
questions.explanation: The course states that the Von Neumann architecture is the foundation for nearly all modern computers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four major subsystems of the Von Neumann architecture?
questions.explanation: The four major subsystems are memory, input/output, the ALU, and the control unit. Cache is not one of the four.

questions.prompt: Which two components are commonly combined to form the CPU:
questions.explanation: The ALU and control unit are often bundled inside the central processing unit (CPU).

questions.prompt: The ALU and the _____ are often bundled inside the central processing unit (CPU).
questions.explanation: The course says the ALU and control unit are often bundled inside the central processing unit (CPU); memory and I/O are separate subsystems.

questions.prompt: Which device would you find in the I/O group of a computer system?
questions.explanation: Input/output is one of the four subsystems; a keyboard is an input device. The ALU and PC are in the CPU, and cache is memory.

questions.prompt: In the Von Neumann architecture, memory is bundled inside the CPU together with the ALU and the control unit.
questions.explanation: The CPU contains only the control unit and the ALU; memory and input-output are separate subsystems.

questions.prompt: The von Neumann architecture ___
options: uses a single bus for data and instructions
uses separate memories for data and instructions
executes sequentially without a program counter
questions.explanation: All subsystems connect to one bus, and programs are stored in the same memory as data (stored program). It has a PC and an ALU.

questions.prompt: Which statement about random access memory (RAM) is correct?
options: Cells near address 0 are accessed faster than other cells
It takes equal time to access any cell
Its cell values can be read but never changed
All of its cells share one common address
questions.explanation: RAM is organized into cells with unique addresses, takes equal time to access any cell, and its cell values may be read and changed.

questions.prompt: Read-only memory (ROM) is:
options: A fast but expensive memory built into the CPU
A register that holds the address of the next instruction
A type of RAM with prerecorded information that cannot be modified or changed
A memory whose cell values may be read and changed
questions.explanation: ROM is a type of RAM with prerecorded information that cannot be modified or changed.

questions.prompt: The values stored in ROM may be read and changed just like the values in ordinary RAM.
questions.explanation: ROM holds prerecorded information that cannot be modified or changed.

questions.prompt: The cell size (memory width) is typically:
questions.explanation: The course says cell size/memory width is typically 8 bits.

questions.prompt: If N is the length of the address, the maximum memory size (address space) is:
questions.explanation: Maximum memory size/address space is 2 to the power N, where N is the length of the address.

questions.prompt: In 3-bit memory addresses, how many memory locations can it access?
questions.explanation: Maximum memory size is \(2^N\) where N is the address length: \(2^3 = 8\) locations (addresses 000 to 111).

questions.prompt: In 8-bit memory addresses, how many memory locations can it access?
questions.explanation: Maximum memory size is \(2^N\): \(2^8 = 256\) locations (addresses 0 to 255).

questions.prompt: If the maximum memory size is 64 memory cells, what is the length N of the memory address?
questions.explanation: Maximum memory size is \(2^N\), where N is the length of the address: \(2^6 = 64\), so N = 6 bits.

questions.title: Match each type of memory/storage with its description

pairs.right: Equal time to access any cell; values may be read and changed
Prerecorded information that cannot be modified or changed
Fast but expensive; built into the CPU
Nonvolatile; disks store sectors of data stored in tracks

questions.prompt: If memory addresses are 16 bits long, the maximum memory size is:
questions.explanation: The table gives N = 16 a maximum memory size of 2^16 = 65,536.

questions.prompt: A computer with 32-bit memory addresses can access a maximum of how many memory cells?
questions.explanation: The table gives N = 32 a maximum memory size of 2^32 = 4,294,967,296.

questions.prompt: Fetch is called a nondestructive operation because:
options: It writes a new value into the memory cell
It erases the cell after reading it
It retrieves a value from memory without changing the cell
questions.explanation: Fetch means retrieve from memory, and it is a nondestructive fetch: the cell keeps its value.

questions.prompt: Which memory operation is described as destructive?
questions.explanation: Store writes to memory (destructive store), replacing the old value of the cell.

questions.prompt: _____ register holds the address of the memory location to be accessed.
questions.explanation: The memory address register (MAR) holds the memory address to access.

questions.prompt: _____ register receives data from a fetch and holds data to be stored.
questions.explanation: The memory data register (MDR) receives data from fetch and holds data to be stored.

questions.prompt: The memory data register (MDR) holds the memory address to be accessed.
questions.explanation: That is the MAR. The MDR receives data from fetch and holds data to be stored.

questions.prompt: What does machine instruction 'STORE 11' do?
options: Writes a value into the memory cell with address 11
Retrieves the value of memory cell 11 without changing it
Puts the number 11 into the program counter
Sends the value 11 to the I/O controller
questions.explanation: Store means write to memory (destructive store), and 11 is the address field telling which memory address to operate on.

questions.prompt: After the instruction 'STORE 20' is executed, what happens to the old value in memory cell 20?
options: It is kept, and the new value is added to it
It is moved to memory cell 21
It is moved to a storage device
It is lost, because store is a destructive operation
questions.explanation: Store means write to memory (destructive store): the new value replaces the old one, and the old content is lost.

questions.prompt: In a store operation, the memory address goes into the _____ and the data to be stored goes into the _____.
questions.explanation: The MAR holds the memory address to access; the MDR receives data from a fetch and holds data to be stored.

questions.prompt: Which circuit converts the MAR into a signal to a specific memory cell?
questions.explanation: The decoder converts the MAR into a signal to a specific memory cell.

questions.prompt: The fetch/store controller acts as the "traffic cop" for which register?
questions.explanation: The fetch/store controller is the traffic cop for the MDR, routing data to/from memory cells and the MDR.

questions.prompt: The decoder is the circuit that routes data flow between the memory cells and the MDR.
questions.explanation: Routing data to/from memory cells and the MDR is the job of the fetch/store controller; the decoder converts the MAR into a signal to a cell.

questions.prompt: In 4-bit memory addresses, how many memory locations can it access?
questions.explanation: With N = 4, the decoder has 2^4 = 16 output lines, addresses 0000 (0) to 1111 (15).

questions.prompt: For a MAR with 4 bits, the memory uses a decoder circuit of type:
questions.explanation: 4 input lines from the MAR and 2^4 = 16 output lines: a 4-to-16 decoder circuit.

questions.prompt: In the two-dimensional memory organization, a memory cell is selected by:
options: A separate selection line for every cell
A row selection line and a column selection line
questions.explanation: Two-dimensional memory organized by row selection lines and column selection lines.

questions.prompt: With 4-bit memory addresses, what is the address of the last memory cell?
questions.explanation: Cells are numbered 0 to \(2^N - 1\). With N = 4 the last address is 1111 = 15 (there are 16 cells, 0 to 15).

questions.prompt: Why is cache memory used in computers?
options: Because it is fast and helps the CPU get data quickly
Because it is cheaper than RAM
Because it holds the address of the next instruction
questions.explanation: Cache memory is fast (but expensive) and is built into the CPU for fast access times.

questions.prompt: Cache memory became necessary mainly because:
options: CPU speeds increased more slowly than RAM speeds
RAM speeds increased more slowly than CPU speeds
RAM cell values cannot be changed
I/O devices became faster than the CPU
questions.explanation: The course says RAM speeds increased more slowly than CPU speeds, so fast cache is built into the CPU.

questions.prompt: The principle of locality states that:
options: Every memory cell takes equal time to access
Values far from recently accessed memory are more likely to be accessed
Values close to recently accessed memory are more likely to be accessed
Each memory cell is given a unique address
questions.explanation: Principle of locality: values close to recently accessed memory are more likely to be accessed.

questions.prompt: Using the principle of locality, the neighbors of accessed values are loaded into cache and recent values are kept there.
questions.explanation: The course says: load neighbors into cache and keep recent values there.

questions.title: Match each memory term with its meaning

pairs.right: Values near recently accessed memory are likely to be accessed
Percentage of times values are found in cache

questions.prompt: Cache memory is:
options: Slow but cheap, and built into the hard disk
Fast but expensive, and built into the CPU
A type of ROM that cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Cache memory is fast but expensive; it is built into the CPU for fast access times.

questions.prompt: Which part of the CPU performs mathematical operations:
questions.explanation: The ALU contains circuits for arithmetic: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

questions.prompt: The data path describes:
options: How information flows in the ALU, from registers to circuits and back to registers
How the MAR is converted into a signal to a memory cell
The order of the fetch, decode, and execute phases
How the program counter is increased by 1
questions.explanation: Data path: how information flows in the ALU, from registers to circuits and from circuits back to registers.

questions.title: Match each part of the ALU with its description

pairs.right: High-speed, dedicated memory connected to circuits
How information flows in the ALU

questions.prompt: Which part of the CPU performs comparison and logic operations such as equality, AND, OR, and NOT?
questions.explanation: The ALU contains circuits for arithmetic and circuits for comparison and logic (equality, and, or, not).

questions.prompt: In the three-register ALU organization, registers A and B ___, and register C ___.
options: receive the result; holds the two inputs
hold the two inputs to the ALU; receives the result
hold memory addresses; holds the op code
hold the address of the next instruction; holds the current instruction
questions.explanation: Registers A and B feeding the ALU, and the ALU output going to register C.

questions.prompt: Programs must be loaded into _____ before they can be executed.
questions.explanation: By the stored program characteristic, programs are stored in memory, where the control unit fetches instructions from.

questions.prompt: The stored program characteristic means that:
options: Programs are stored permanently inside the ALU registers
Programs are stored only in cache memory
Programs are encoded in binary and stored in the computer's memory
Programs are stored on mass storage and executed from there
questions.explanation: Stored program characteristic: programs are encoded in binary and stored in the computer's memory.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the control unit in a computer?
options: It performs arithmetic and logic operations
It fetches, decodes, and executes instructions
It stores data and programs permanently
It converts the MAR into a signal to a memory cell
questions.explanation: The control unit fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and executes them.

questions.prompt: In an encoded instruction, the operation code (op code) tells:
options: Which memory addresses/registers to operate on
The address of the next instruction
How many bits each memory cell has
questions.explanation: The op code tells which operation; the addresses tell which memory addresses/registers to operate on.

questions.prompt: In the machine instruction 'STORE 11', the number 11 is:
options: The memory address to operate on
The number of times the instruction is repeated
questions.explanation: Encoded instructions have an op code (which operation: STORE) and addresses (which memory addresses/registers to operate on: 11).

questions.prompt: In the machine instruction 'STORE 11', the part 'STORE' is the:
questions.explanation: The operation code (op code) tells which operation to perform (store = write to memory); 11 is the address.

questions.prompt: Which unit fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and executes them?
questions.explanation: The control unit fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and executes them; the ALU performs the computations.

questions.prompt: The ALU fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and executes them.
questions.explanation: That is the control unit. The ALU contains the arithmetic, comparison and logic circuits and performs computations.

questions.prompt: The stored program characteristic of the Von Neumann architecture means that programs are encoded in binary and stored in the computer's memory.
questions.explanation: The course states the stored program characteristic: programs are encoded in binary and stored in the computer's memory.

questions.prompt: In machine language, sequences of instructions encode algorithms.
questions.explanation: The course says sequences of instructions encode algorithms.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an instruction set in a processor?
options: It stores the data the processor is working on
It speeds up memory access by keeping recent values
It holds the address of the next instruction
It tells the processor which operations it can perform
questions.explanation: An instruction set is the set of instructions implemented by a particular chip, i.e. The operations it can perform.

questions.prompt: Why can machine language written for one kind of processor not run directly on a different kind of processor?
options: Each kind of processor has a different instruction set (speaks a different language)
Different processors use different cell sizes
Machine language cannot be carried out by hardware
Only RISC processors can run machine language
questions.explanation: The course says each kind of processor has a different instruction set, so it speaks a different language.

questions.prompt: Which is a characteristic of RISC?
options: Small instruction set with each instruction highly optimized
A single instruction can do a lot of work
questions.explanation: RISC: small instruction sets, each instruction highly optimized, easy to design hardware.

questions.prompt: Which is a characteristic of CISC?
options: A single instruction can do a lot of work
questions.explanation: CISC: large instruction set, single instruction can do a lot of work, complex to design hardware.

questions.prompt: Modern hardware is:
options: A compromise between RISC and CISC
questions.explanation: The course says modern hardware is a compromise between RISC and CISC.

questions.prompt: CISC has a large instruction set and its hardware is complex to design.
questions.explanation: CISC: large instruction set, single instruction can do a lot of work, complex to design hardware.

questions.prompt: In RISC, a single instruction can do a lot of work.
questions.explanation: That describes CISC. RISC has small instruction sets with each instruction highly optimized.

questions.title: Match each term with its description

pairs.right: Small instruction set; each instruction highly optimized
Large instruction set; one instruction can do a lot of work
Instructions implemented by a particular chip

questions.prompt: A large instruction set in which a single instruction can do a lot of work, with complex-to-design hardware, describes:
questions.explanation: Complex instruction set computer (CISC): large instruction set, single instruction can do a lot of work, complex to design hardware.

questions.prompt: Small instruction sets, each instruction highly optimized, and easy-to-design hardware describe:
questions.explanation: Reduced instruction set computer (RISC): small instruction sets, each instruction highly optimized, easy to design hardware.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly differentiates between RISC and CISC?
options: RISC has a large instruction set; CISC has a small instruction set
In RISC a single instruction can do a lot of work; in CISC each instruction is highly optimized
RISC has a small instruction set and easy-to-design hardware; CISC has a large instruction set and complex-to-design hardware
RISC hardware is complex to design; CISC hardware is easy to design
questions.explanation: RISC: small instruction sets, highly optimized instructions, easy hardware. CISC: large instruction set, one instruction does a lot of work, complex hardware.

questions.prompt: RISC stands for:
questions.explanation: RISC = Reduced instruction set computer; CISC = Complex instruction set computer.

questions.prompt: Modern hardware is a compromise between RISC and CISC.
questions.explanation: The course says modern hardware is a compromise between RISC and CISC.

questions.prompt: The program counter (PC) register holds:
options: The encoding of the current instruction
The data received from a fetch
The address of the next instruction
questions.explanation: The PC register holds the address of the next instruction.

questions.prompt: _____ holds the encoding of the current instruction.
questions.explanation: The instruction register (IR) holds the encoding of the current instruction.

questions.prompt: The instruction decoder circuit:
options: Converts the MAR into a signal to a specific memory cell
Decodes the op code of an instruction and signals helper circuits, one per instruction
Routes data flow to/from memory cells and the MDR
Holds the address of the next instruction
questions.explanation: The instruction decoder circuit decodes the op code and signals helper circuits, one per instruction.

questions.title: Match each register with what it holds

pairs.right: Data from a fetch or data to be stored
The address of the next instruction
The encoding of the current instruction

questions.prompt: _____ register holds the address of the next instruction.
questions.explanation: The program counter (PC) register holds the address of the next instruction; the IR holds the current instruction.

questions.prompt: The instruction register (IR) is divided into which two parts?
questions.explanation: The IR made of the op code and the address field(s).

questions.prompt: The fetch/decode/execute phase is also called:
questions.explanation: The fetch/decode/execute phase is also called the Von Neumann cycle.

questions.prompt: A Von Neumann machine repeats the fetch/decode/execute phase until:
options: A HALT instruction or an error
questions.explanation: The machine repeats the cycle until a HALT instruction or error.

questions.prompt: In which phase does the instruction decoder get the op code?
questions.explanation: Decode phase: the instruction decoder gets the op code.

questions.prompt: The execute phase is the same for every instruction.
questions.explanation: The course says the execute phase is different for each instruction.

questions.title: Match each part of the Von Neumann cycle with its description

pairs.right: Instruction decoder gets the op code

questions.prompt: The correct order of the phases of the Von Neumann cycle is:
questions.explanation: The fetch/decode/execute phase (Von Neumann cycle) runs in this order: fetch phase, then decode phase (the instruction decoder gets the op code), then execute phase.

questions.prompt: A Von Neumann machine repeats the fetch/decode/execute cycle until a HALT instruction or an error.
questions.explanation: The course says the machine repeats the fetch/decode/execute phase until a HALT instruction or error.

questions.prompt: In the organization of a Von Neumann computer, the MAR, the MDR, and the fetch/store controller belong to which unit?
questions.explanation: MAR, MDR, memory decoder circuits, and the fetch/store controller in the memory unit.

questions.prompt: In the organization of a Von Neumann computer, which components belong to the control unit?
options: PC, IR, and the instruction decoder circuit
MAR, MDR, and the fetch/store controller
Registers R0-R3 and the condition code register
The I/O controller and the I/O device
questions.explanation: The PC, IR, and instruction decoder circuit in the control unit.

questions.prompt: The Von Neumann bottleneck is:
options: The percentage of times values are found in cache
The inability of sequential machines to handle larger problems
The slowness of RAM compared to cache
The limit on memory size set by the address length
questions.explanation: Von Neumann bottleneck: inability of sequential machines to handle larger problems.

questions.prompt: Why can chips not keep getting faster by putting gates much closer together?
options: Signals through wire are limited by the speed of light, and heat production increases too fast
Gates cannot be built from transistors
RAM speeds increased faster than CPU speeds
questions.explanation: The course says the speed of light pertains to signals through wire, gates cannot be put much closer, and heat production increases too fast.

questions.prompt: What is parallel processing?
options: One processing unit executing instructions one after another
Many processing units operating at the same time
Loading the neighbors of recent values into cache
Organizing memory into rows and columns
questions.explanation: Parallel processing: many processing units operating at the same time.

questions.prompt: Most non-Von Neumann architectures are experimental/theoretical. Which one is the exception?
questions.explanation: The course says most non-Von Neumann architectures are experimental/theoretical, EXCEPT parallel processing.

questions.title: Match each period with its example of parallel processing

pairs.right: Desktop multicore machines and the cloud

questions.prompt: Parallel processing is a non-Von Neumann architecture.
questions.explanation: Non-Von Neumann architectures are other ways to organize computers; most are experimental/theoretical, EXCEPT parallel processing.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly states two properties of the Von Neumann architecture?
options: Data and instructions use separate memories, and there is no control unit
Many processing units operate at the same time, and there is no memory
Programs are stored in memory, and execution is sequential unless the program says otherwise
Programs are stored in the ALU, and instructions execute in random order
questions.explanation: The summary says Von Neumann machines have memory, I/O, ALU, and control unit; programs are stored in memory; execution is sequential unless the program says otherwise.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a property of the Von Neumann architecture?
options: Execution is sequential unless the program says otherwise
It has four subsystems: memory, I/O, ALU, and control unit
Many processing units operate at the same time
questions.explanation: Von Neumann machines store programs in memory and execute sequentially. Many processing units operating at the same time is parallel processing, a non-Von Neumann architecture.

questions.title: Match each Von Neumann subsystem with its role

pairs.right: Functional unit where data is stored/retrieved
Slow; needs a dedicated controller to free the CPU

questions.prompt: Parallel processing architectures can perform multiple instructions at one time.
questions.explanation: The summary says parallel processing architectures can perform multiple instructions at one time.

questions.prompt: According to the summary, mass data storage is:
questions.explanation: The summary says mass data storage is nonvolatile.

questions.prompt: Why does I/O need a dedicated controller?
options: I/O is faster than the CPU
The controller decodes op codes for the CPU
The controller holds the address of the next instruction
I/O is slow, so the controller frees the CPU
questions.explanation: The summary says I/O is slow and needs a dedicated controller to free the CPU.
